name: Earth
summary: From Earth’s assembly out of the early Solar System to a biologically transformed planet with plate tectonics, oceans, atmospheric oxygen, forests, and complex ecosystems.
climate: Hadean heat gave way to liquid-water oceans, fluctuating greenhouse climates, global glaciations, and today’s interglacial.
geo: Earth differentiated into a core, mantle and crust. Tectonics assembled and dispersed supercontinents repeatedly.
continents: Continental crust developed over billions of years. Ocean basins have repeatedly opened and closed.
life: Life was microbial for most of Earth’s history; multicellular organisms and land ecosystems diversified relatively recently.
etym: Earth: from Old English eorþe, “ground, soil, world.”
events: ≥3.5 Ga: strong evidence of microbial life
~2.4 Ga: major rise in atmospheric oxygen

name: Hadean
etym: Named for Hades, Greek realm of the dead, evoking an early high-energy Earth.
summary: Earth forms from the solar nebula. Core segregation, impacts and early crust formation establish the conditions for oceans.
climate: Initially extremely hot, later cooler enough for solid crust and likely surface water in portions of the eon.
continents: No stable modern-style continents; early crust was repeatedly reworked.
geo: Giant impacts, magma oceans, core formation, oldest surviving zircons (~4.4 Ga).
life: No confirmed life from the Hadean.
events: ~4.4 Ga: ancient zircons imply low-temperature interaction with water

name: Archean
etym: Greek arkhaîos, “ancient, original.”
summary: Earth’s earliest large-scale biological record: microbial mats, oxygenic photosynthesis and growing continental nuclei.

continents: Small continental nuclei and greenstone belts, with tectonic regimes still debated.
geo: Cratons and granite-greenstone terranes develop, and banded iron formations accumulate.
life: Bacteria and archaea thrive; photosynthetic microbial ecosystems expand.
events: Early oxygenic photosynthesis before atmospheric oxygenation

life: Eukaryotes, algae and multicellularity become established; Ediacaran organisms appear late.
